meta.title: Solution Sets to Inequalities with Two Variables
meta.description: Graph linear inequalities in two variables as shaded half-planes with solid or dashed boundary lines.
meta.pageDescription: Graph linear inequalities in two variables, use test points, and shade feasible half-planes.
meta.author: Hesten's Learning Team

overview.title: Student & Teacher Overview: Lesson 21
overview.text: In this lesson, you will graph linear inequalities in two variables (such as $y < 2x - 1$ or $Ax + By \ge C$). A linear boundary divides the Cartesian plane into two half-planes. You will master using a test point (such as $(0, 0)$) to decide which half-plane contains the solutions.
outcomes: Graph the solution set to a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane.
Differentiate between solid boundary lines (inclusive $\le, \ge$) and dashed boundary lines (strict $<, >$).
Select and evaluate a test point (e.g., $(0, 0)$) to identify which side of the boundary to shade.
overview.teacherInsight: Highlight that if the boundary line passes through the origin $(0, 0)$, students must select an alternate test point like $(0, 1)$ or $(1, 0)$ to test which half-plane to shade.

content.html:
Rules for Graphing Two-Variable Inequalities

Boundary Line Style

$$\text{Strict } (<, >): \text{Dashed} \quad | \quad \text{Inclusive } (\le, \ge): \text{Solid}$$

Solid lines include points on the boundary; dashed lines indicate the boundary itself is excluded from solutions.

Test-Point Verification

$$\text{Test } (0, 0) \to \text{If True: Shade Origin Side}$$

If $(0,0)$ evaluates to True, shade the side containing $(0,0)$. If False, shade the opposite side.

vocabulary.definition: The region of a coordinate plane on one side of an infinite boundary line.
The line dividing the coordinate plane into two half-planes in an inequality graph.
A coordinate pair (not on the boundary line) substituted into an inequality to determine which half-plane contains solutions.

practiceQuestions.question: Which boundary line style and shading represents $y > 2x + 1$?
options: A dashed boundary line, shaded ABOVE the line
A solid boundary line, shaded ABOVE the line
A dashed boundary line, shaded BELOW the line
A solid boundary line, shaded BELOW the line
practiceQuestions.explanation: Because $>$ is strict, the boundary is dashed. Testing $(0, 0)$: $0 > 2(0) + 1 \implies 0 > 1$ (False). The region not containing $(0, 0)$—above the line—is shaded.

practiceQuestions.question: Is the point $(2, 3)$ in the solution set of $3x - y \ge 3$?
options: Yes, because $3(2) - 3 = 3 \ge 3$ is a true statement.
No, because $3$ is not strictly greater than 3.
No, because $(2, 3)$ is in the first quadrant.
Yes, but only if the line is dashed.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Substitute $(2, 3)$: $3(2) - 3 = 6 - 3 = 3$. Since $3 \ge 3$ is True (equality is permitted), $(2, 3)$ is on the boundary and is a valid solution.
